records.description:
(PDF) Painters from Western Macedonia active in the Romanian Principalities. The brothers Ioannis and Georgios (floruerunt c. 1640-1655)

# Painters from Western Macedonia active in the Romanian Principalities. The brothers Ioannis and Georgios (floruerunt c. 1640-1655)

Elisabeta Negrău

Elisabeta Negrău

2020, DChAE (Deltion tes Christianikes Archaiologikes Hetaireias), vol. 41

Abstract

The study analyses the works of two virtually unknown Greek painters from the mid-seventeenth century. The names of the two painters, the brothers Ioannis and Georgios, are known from a letter addressed to Patriarch Nikon of Moscow, dated July 25 1655, in which they enumerate several churches they painted in Kiev and Wallachia: Berestovo, Căldărușani, Brebu, Strehaia, Cornățel, Plumbuita, Plătărești, Soveja. The study concludes that the two painters were trained in (nowadays) Western Macedonia. It also discusses the connections between the two painters, their patrons and the theologian Meletios Syrigos.

## Abstract
sparkles
AI
The study explores the complexities surrounding John the Grammarian (Ioannis VII), a significant yet contentious figure in the history of Byzantine science and culture during the Middle Byzantine period. It emphasizes the dual challenges of interpreting historical scientific discourse and the scarcity of reliable data. The analysis highlights the political, ideological, and social factors influencing scientific activity and knowledge, particularly through the lens of John's role in the iconoclast controversy and his subsequent historiography. The paper aims to reconstruct John's intellectual contributions and the external perceptions that shaped his legacy.
... Read more
## Key takeaways
sparkles
AI
1. John VII The Grammarian illustrates the complex interplay between science, ideology, and politics in Middle Byzantine society.
2. His scientific interests were perceived as heretical, leading to accusations of magic and association with the Devil.
3. Ioannis' diplomatic mission to Baghdad in the 830s showcased Byzantine interest in rediscovering ancient Greek sciences.
4. The patriarch's expulsion in 843 exemplifies the consequences of ideological conflicts during the iconoclast crisis.
5. Literary portrayals reflect the era's stigma against scientific inquiry, linking it with occult practices and atheism.

The Avicennan text De congelatione et conglutinatione lapidum had a great influence on the alchemical thought of the thirteenth century. This Latin text disputed both the veracity of alchemy and the possibility of alchemical transmutation by arguing that art is inferior to nature and that the alchemists cannot manipulate a metal because its true characteristics are hidden from our senses; thus an alchemist cannot change something which is unknown to him. Newman's pioneer studies examined the diffusion and impact of the first Avicennan argument on medieval alchemy and he shed light on the art-versus-nature debate. This paper has a twofold aim: on the one hand it aims to further Newman's study by focusing on the second Avicennan argument, which is closely related to the problem of substantial form, and on the other hand it aims to show how the aforesaid problem paved the way for the emergence of corpuscularianism, which flourished during the early modern period. In this regard, it will become clear that the historiographical case of alchemy and its problem of substantial form can serve as an exegetical tool for 'bridging' the Middle Ages and the early modern period with respect to the relation between Aristotelianism and corpuscularianism.

An article concerning approaches to the concept of 'grammar' during Byzantine centuries. Grammar was acknowledged as a valuable aspect from inherited ancient Greek philological and grammatical tradition and also a valuable tool for commenting on and interpreting both ancient Greek and Biblical texts. First, as the primary crucial stage of the enkýklios paideía, grammar was treated as the absolutely essential apparatus for accessing higher levels of knowledge, such as rhetoric and philosophy. Furthermore, grammar was seen to provide readers with the ability to comprehend the Word of God and the Scriptures, since those texts were not written in vernacular. ln addition, older treatments of etymology were believed to convey ancient theoretical linguistic thought. Finally, grammar was valued for connecting Byzantine Greeks with the glorious past, revealing to them the mythical and allegorical content of earlier texts, a connection that became especially precious in view of the Ottoman occupation.

Anna Usacheva

In late antiquity, the questions concerning the nature and origin of language surfaced in discussions of religious thinkers. Touching upon the concepts of prayer, exegesis of the sacred texts, and divine names, linguistic issues featured in the works of Origen. Thus, the first book of his Contra Celsum preserves an intriguing account of the classical and contemporary language theories. Daniélou and Dillon considered this Origen’s witness as a proof of his sympathies to the voces magicae concept, which goes back to the Chaldean Oracles. In this article, I examine the reliability of Origen’s doxographical testimony, sketch his linguistic views in the context of the Stoic teaching and show what practical implications his language theory had on his approach to exegesis and prayer. # Painters from Western Macedonia active in the Romanian Principalities. The brothers Ioannis and Georgios (floruerunt c. 1640-1655)

Elisabeta Negrău

Elisabeta Negrău

2020, DChAE (Deltion tes Christianikes Archaiologikes Hetaireias), vol. 41

Abstract

The study analyses the works of two virtually unknown Greek painters from the mid-seventeenth century. The names of the two painters, the brothers Ioannis and Georgios, are known from a letter addressed to Patriarch Nikon of Moscow, dated July 25 1655, in which they enumerate several churches they painted in Kiev and Wallachia: Berestovo, Căldărușani, Brebu, Strehaia, Cornățel, Plumbuita, Plătărești, Soveja. The study concludes that the two painters were trained in (nowadays) Western Macedonia. It also discusses the connections between the two painters, their patrons and the theologian Meletios Syrigos.

## Abstract
sparkles
AI
The study explores the complexities surrounding John the Grammarian (Ioannis VII), a significant yet contentious figure in the history of Byzantine science and culture during the Middle Byzantine period. It emphasizes the dual challenges of interpreting historical scientific discourse and the scarcity of reliable data. The analysis highlights the political, ideological, and social factors influencing scientific activity and knowledge, particularly through the lens of John's role in the iconoclast controversy and his subsequent historiography. The paper aims to reconstruct John's intellectual contributions and the external perceptions that shaped his legacy.
... Read more
## Key takeaways
sparkles
AI
1. John VII The Grammarian illustrates the complex interplay between science, ideology, and politics in Middle Byzantine society.
2. His scientific interests were perceived as heretical, leading to accusations of magic and association with the Devil.
3. Ioannis' diplomatic mission to Baghdad in the 830s showcased Byzantine interest in rediscovering ancient Greek sciences.
4. The patriarch's expulsion in 843 exemplifies the consequences of ideological conflicts during the iconoclast crisis.
5. Literary portrayals reflect the era's stigma against scientific inquiry, linking it with occult practices and atheism.

The Avicennan text De congelatione et conglutinatione lapidum had a great influence on the alchemical thought of the thirteenth century. This Latin text disputed both the veracity of alchemy and the possibility of alchemical transmutation by arguing that art is inferior to nature and that the alchemists cannot manipulate a metal because its true characteristics are hidden from our senses; thus an alchemist cannot change something which is unknown to him. Newman's pioneer studies examined the diffusion and impact of the first Avicennan argument on medieval alchemy and he shed light on the art-versus-nature debate. In this regard, it will become clear that the historiographical case of alchemy and its problem of substantial form can serve as an exegetical tool for 'bridging' the Middle Ages and the early modern period with respect to the relation between Aristotelianism and corpuscularianism.

An article concerning approaches to the concept of 'grammar' during Byzantine centuries. Grammar was acknowledged as a valuable aspect from inherited ancient Greek philological and grammatical tradition and also a valuable tool for commenting on and interpreting both ancient Greek and Biblical texts. First, as the primary crucial stage of the enkýklios paideía, grammar was treated as the absolutely essential apparatus for accessing higher levels of knowledge, such as rhetoric and philosophy. Furthermore, grammar was seen to provide readers with the ability to comprehend the Word of God and the Scriptures, since those texts were not written in vernacular. ln addition, older treatments of etymology were believed to convey ancient theoretical linguistic thought. Finally, grammar was valued for connecting Byzantine Greeks with the glorious past, revealing to them the mythical and allegorical content of earlier texts, a connection that became especially precious in view of the Ottoman occupation.

sparkles

What explains John the Grammarian's portrayal as a magician in Byzantine sources?add
The paper reveals that Byzantine chroniclers labeled Ioannis as a magician due to his opposition to icons, associating him with diabolic characteristics, including the appellation 'Hylilas', linked to the Devil.
How did John the Grammarian influence the educational framework of Byzantine society?add
The study finds that Ioannis significantly impacted Byzantine education by mentoring Emperor Theophilus and facilitating a revival of interest in sciences, leading to the establishment of the imperial school at Magnaura.
What methodologies did John use to gather knowledge during his research?add
Ioannis systematically searched texts in monastery libraries for lost works, such as those burned in the 782 Council, showcasing a dedicated archival approach to reconstruct the historical discourse on sciences.
When did John the Grammarian serve as a key political figure in the Byzantine Empire?add
Ioannis ascended to prominence when appointed as teacher to Emperor Theophilus around 829, influencing the emperor's favorable stance toward scientific advancement amid religious conflict.
Why was John's scientific interest perceived negatively during the iconoclast period?add
The paper discusses how Ioannis's scientific pursuits were conflated with heresy, leading to accusations of atheism and magic, reflecting broader ideological battles within the politically charged atmosphere of the time.

# Painters from Western Macedonia active in the Romanian Principalities. The brothers Ioannis and Georgios (floruerunt c. 1640-1655)

Elisabeta Negrău

Elisabeta Negrău

2020, DChAE (Deltion tes Christianikes Archaiologikes Hetaireias), vol. 41

Abstract

The study analyses the works of two virtually unknown Greek painters from the mid-seventeenth century. The names of the two painters, the brothers Ioannis and Georgios, are known from a letter addressed to Patriarch Nikon of Moscow, dated July 25 1655, in which they enumerate several churches they painted in Kiev and Wallachia: Berestovo, Căldărușani, Brebu, Strehaia, Cornățel, Plumbuita, Plătărești, Soveja. The study concludes that the two painters were trained in (nowadays) Western Macedonia. It also discusses the connections between the two painters, their patrons and the theologian Meletios Syrigos.

## Abstract
sparkles
AI
The study explores the complexities surrounding John the Grammarian (Ioannis VII), a significant yet contentious figure in the history of Byzantine science and culture during the Middle Byzantine period. It emphasizes the dual challenges of interpreting historical scientific discourse and the scarcity of reliable data. The analysis highlights the political, ideological, and social factors influencing scientific activity and knowledge, particularly through the lens of John's role in the iconoclast controversy and his subsequent historiography. The paper aims to reconstruct John's intellectual contributions and the external perceptions that shaped his legacy.

## Key takeaways
sparkles
AI
1. John VII The Grammarian illustrates the complex interplay between science, ideology, and politics in Middle Byzantine society.
2. His scientific interests were perceived as heretical, leading to accusations of magic and association with the Devil.
3. Ioannis' diplomatic mission to Baghdad in the 830s showcased Byzantine interest in rediscovering ancient Greek sciences.
4. The patriarch's expulsion in 843 exemplifies the consequences of ideological conflicts during the iconoclast crisis.
5. Literary portrayals reflect the era's stigma against scientific inquiry, linking it with occult practices and atheism.

Athanasios Rinotas
Rinotas, A. (2025). Aristotelianism, alchemy and corpuscularianism in the thirteenth century: the problem of substantial form and its corpuscular solution. The British Journal for the History of Science, 1–17, 2025
The Avicennan text De congelatione et conglutinatione lapidum had a great influence on the alchemical thought of the thirteenth century. This Latin text disputed both the veracity of alchemy and the possibility of alchemical transmutation by arguing that art is inferior to nature and that the alchemists cannot manipulate a metal because its true characteristics are hidden from our senses; thus an alchemist cannot change something which is unknown to him. Newman's pioneer studies examined the diffusion and impact of the first Avicennan argument on medieval alchemy and he shed light on the art-versus-nature debate. This paper has a twofold aim: on the one hand it aims to further Newman's study by focusing on the second Avicennan argument, which is closely related to the problem of substantial form, and on the other hand it aims to show how the aforesaid problem paved the way for the emergence of corpuscularianism, which flourished during the early modern period. In this regard, it will become clear that the historiographical case of alchemy and its problem of substantial form can serve as an exegetical tool for 'bridging' the Middle Ages and the early modern period with respect to the relation between Aristotelianism and corpuscularianism.

Grammatical Thought in Byzantium
Maria Chriti
Brill's Encyclopedia of Ancient Greek Language and Linguistics, 2026
An article concerning approaches to the concept of 'grammar' during Byzantine centuries. Grammar was acknowledged as a valuable aspect from inherited ancient Greek philological and grammatical tradition and also a valuable tool for commenting on and interpreting both ancient Greek and Biblical texts. First, as the primary crucial stage of the enkýklios paideía, grammar was treated as the absolutely essential apparatus for accessing higher levels of knowledge, such as rhetoric and philosophy. Furthermore, grammar was seen to provide readers with the ability to comprehend the Word of God and the Scriptures, since those texts were not written in vernacular. ln addition, older treatments of etymology were believed to convey ancient theoretical linguistic thought. Finally, grammar was valued for connecting Byzantine Greeks with the glorious past, revealing to them the mythical and allegorical content of earlier texts, a connection that became especially precious in view of the Ottoman occupation.

Dire le Sacré chez Origène: Language Theory of Origen and the Voces Magicae Concept in the Context of Late Antiquity
Anna Usacheva
The article is forthcoming in: A-A. Morello, V. Michel-Fauré, M. Jacquemier (eds.), Dire le sacré: spiritualités et représentations (musique, arts visuels, littérature, philosophie, théologie), Collection Plantin. Beauchesne (forthcoming in 2018).
In late antiquity, the questions concerning the nature and origin of language surfaced in discussions of religious thinkers. Touching upon the concepts of prayer, exegesis of the sacred texts, and divine names, linguistic issues featured in the works of Origen. Thus, the first book of his Contra Celsum preserves an intriguing account of the classical and contemporary language theories. Daniélou and Dillon considered this Origen’s witness as a proof of his sympathies to the voces magicae concept, which goes back to the Chaldean Oracles. In this article, I examine the reliability of Origen’s doxographical testimony, sketch his linguistic views in the context of the Stoic teaching and show what practical implications his language theory had on his approach to exegesis and prayer. Keywords: Origen, the voces magicae concept, Stoic etymological theory, the issue of the correctness of names, the lekton concept.

# The Empire Strikes Back: Multi-Faith Cyprus and Byzantine Orthodox Culture in Seventeenth-Century Eastern Mediterranean, Cerae 8 (2021), 3-34

Chrysovalantis Kyriacou

## Abstract

The aim of this paper is to explore ways in which Byzantine symbols, ideas, and practices constituted a transcultural ‘language’ of communication for groups of Christians in Ottoman-ruled Cyprus in the seventeenth century. Aspects of this koine are sometimes visible in the contacts between Cypriot Christians and Western Europeans (mainly Catholics, but also Lutherans) outside Cyprus, and perhaps also in the interaction between Cypriot Christians and Muslims. The Byzantine koine indicates a process of interaction between Greek and non- Greek cultural agents, through which new and mutually understandable forms of Byzantine culture emerged. records.description:
(PDF) Painters from Western Macedonia active in the Romanian Principalities. The brothers Ioannis and Georgios (floruerunt c. 1640-1655)

# Painters from Western Macedonia active in the Romanian Principalities. The brothers Ioannis and Georgios (floruerunt c. 1640-1655)

Elisabeta Negrău

Elisabeta Negrău

2020, DChAE (Deltion tes Christianikes Archaiologikes Hetaireias), vol. 41

Abstract

The study analyses the works of two virtually unknown Greek painters from the mid-seventeenth century. The names of the two painters, the brothers Ioannis and Georgios, are known from a letter addressed to Patriarch Nikon of Moscow, dated July 25 1655, in which they enumerate several churches they painted in Kiev and Wallachia: Berestovo, Căldărușani, Brebu, Strehaia, Cornățel, Plumbuita, Plătărești, Soveja. The study concludes that the two painters were trained in (nowadays) Western Macedonia. It also discusses the connections between the two painters, their patrons and the theologian Meletios Syrigos.

...

Key takeaways AI generated

1. The study focuses on the works of brothers Ioannis and Georgios, Greek painters from the 17th century.
2. Ioannis and Georgios painted several churches in Kiev and Wallachia, including Căldărușani and Brebu.
3. They were likely trained in Western Macedonia and influenced by local painting traditions.
4. Their work reflects a conservative Orthodox artistic tradition during the reign of Matthew Basarab (1632-1654).
5. The letter to Patriarch Nikon indicates their intent to spread their fresco painting techniques in Russia.

...

What were the primary locations painted by brothers Ioannis and Georgios? add

The paper reveals that Ioannis and Georgios painted numerous churches, including Căldărușani and Brebu, primarily located in Wallachia and Kiev between 1640 and 1655.

How did their training in Macedonia influence their style? add

The study suggests that their Macedonian training introduced conservatism and classical reminiscences in their murals, as evident in juxtaposition with contemporary styles in Wallachia.

When did Ioannis and Georgios start their commissions in Wallachia? add

They likely began working on commissions in Wallachia shortly after 1643, immediately after their completion of murals in Berestovo.

What role did Meletios Syrigos play with these painters? add

Syrigos recommended Ioannis and Georgios to the Metropolitan of Kiev, facilitating their introduction to the Romanian Principalities as skilled fresco painters.

...

## Research claims

Painters Ioannis and Georgios likely began commissions under Matthew Basarab around 1643, indicating early artistic contributions in Wallachia. View claim details arrow_forward

The preference for Northwestern Greek painters by mid-seventeenth-century Romanian church founders is evident through various works commissioned. View claim details arrow_forward

Seventeenth-century Romanian voivodes viewed traditional art as decadent, favoring Baroque aesthetics over established practices. View claim details arrow_forward

## Abstract
sparkles
AI
The study explores the complexities surrounding John the Grammarian (Ioannis VII), a significant yet contentious figure in the history of Byzantine science and culture during the Middle Byzantine period. It emphasizes the dual challenges of interpreting historical scientific discourse and the scarcity of reliable data. The analysis highlights the political, ideological, and social factors influencing scientific activity and knowledge, particularly through the lens of John's role in the iconoclast controversy and his subsequent historiography. The paper aims to reconstruct John's intellectual contributions and the external perceptions that shaped his legacy.
... Read more
## Key takeaways
sparkles
AI
1. John VII The Grammarian illustrates the complex interplay between science, ideology, and politics in Middle Byzantine society.
2. His scientific interests were perceived as heretical, leading to accusations of magic and association with the Devil.
3. Ioannis' diplomatic mission to Baghdad in the 830s showcased Byzantine interest in rediscovering ancient Greek sciences.
4. The patriarch's expulsion in 843 exemplifies the consequences of ideological conflicts during the iconoclast crisis.
5. Literary portrayals reflect the era's stigma against scientific inquiry, linking it with occult practices and atheism.

Grammar was acknowledged as a valuable aspect from inherited ancient Greek philological and grammatical tradition and also a valuable tool for commenting on and interpreting both ancient Greek and Biblical texts. First, as the primary crucial stage of the enkýklios paideía, grammar was treated as the absolutely essential apparatus for accessing higher levels of knowledge, such as rhetoric and philosophy. records.title: (PDF) Classical Antiquity and Cretan Renaissance Poetry
records.description:
The Cretan poets of the Renaissance period were interested in classical antiquity. There can be no dispute about that. It is apparent from the sporadic but significant references and allusions to people, places, myths and events of the ancient world in their poems and dramatic works. But this does not tell us very much. Since the Renaissance movement of which they were part was supremely interested in reviving classical-Greek and Romanculture and in learning from its example, we could not speak of a "Cretan Renaissance," in the sense in which that term is widely used today, if this were not the case. By using the term "Renaissance," we are already implying a conscious relationship with the culture of the ancient world. We can therefore take it as a given, and shift our focus to more qualitative questions. How did the Cretan poets exploit classical material? What sources did they draw on? How did they view the classical past and, most interestingly, how did they relate the culture of ancient Greece and Rome to their view of themselves-their identity? These are some of the questions that need to be considered in an exploration of this fascinating and little researched subject, questions that have an increasing relevance as the phenomenon of the Cretan Renaissance becomes more widely understood and appreciated in the context of modern Greek culture as a whole. records.title: (PDF) Кем был в миру патриарх Иоасаф I (1634–1640 гг.)? // Вестник архивиста. 2023. № 3. С. 651–662.
records.description: The article is devoted to the patriarch Joasaphus I’s (1634–40) origin and status in worldly life. Earlier he was the abbot of the Pskov-Caves Monastery (1621–27) and the Pskov archbishop (1627–34). Joasaphus became the metropolitan after the death of Philaret (Romanov) (1619–33). The researchers noted that they had a close relationship. The only previously known historical source informing of Joasaphus’s origin is the Chronograph of the Astrakhan archbishop Pachomius (mid-17th century). It reports that Joasaphus was a descendant of servitors of Boyar scions (deti boyarskie). His parents’ names in religion (Julia and Bogolep) are known to researchers from the Synodic of the Cornelius Komelski monastery. The author of the article has managed to find new data. Synodic of the Yaroslavl Transfiguration of the Savior Monastery notes Joasaphus’s secular name: Ivan Borisov, son of Tonky (the Thin). The author has also established that, prior to taking his monastic vows (1609), Ivan made a donation (a 16th century manuscript) to the Siya Monastery of St. Antonius to commemorate his parents. In 1601–05 Philaret lived in this monastery in exile. Ivan’s father, Boris (Bogolep), might have lived in this monastery with him. The record of donation mentions Ivan’s status: he was a Boyar scion of the Rostov metropolitan Philaret. Considering absence of the names of Ivan and his father in the list of servitors of the Rostov metropolitan’s house (1591/92), the author supposes that Ivan had been connected with Philaret before the latter became the Rostov metropolitan. Probably he was a servitor of the Romanovs (aristocrats like Fedor Nikitich Romanov had a lot of them). Ivan might have taken the monastic vows in the Solovetsky monastery (ca. 1611–12) after his overlord Philaret had been captured by the Poles. After his returning in Moscow, thanks to his relationship with Philaret, Joasaphus made a successful church career. Ivan/Joasaphus’s interest in books might have been instrumental in this. His donation to the monastery was not typical for a representative of service class people. As a rule, they donated the Gospel, Psalter, Menaion to churches and monasteries. Ivan possibly inherited his interest in books from his father. The Gift book of the Siya Monastery of St. Antonius informs that monk Bogolep (probably, the father of the future patriarch) gave no less than 6 books to the monastery in late 16th century. The research is based on the colophons, Synodics, Commemoration books of the Russian monasteries.

## Abstract

1.1. The work known today as the apocryphal Apocalypsis Ioannis (AI) probably originated in the 5 th -6 th century in Byzantium. Regrettably, the information about it dates from much later, which hinders a more precise chronological placement of its creation: AI is mentioned for the first time in a 9 th century work of Pseudo-Theodosius of Alexandria and the earliest Greek manuscript featuring the text dates from the 12 th century. 1 That is why it was dated on the basis of indirect evidence (terminological and source material) contained in the text itself, which indicates that the work could not have been written before the 5 th century. It is assumed that its Slavonic translation most probably dates from the 10 th century as indicated by the linguistic, textological, literary and historical data in the Slavonic version of AI. 2 1.2. AI is a quaestiones et responsiones work of eschatological content, which is ascribed to the author of the canonical Revelation. It became a basic text for medieval Eastern Orthodox literature by way of intertextual links. Thanks to its literary authority, AI became the source of other works of the most varied origin, genre and status (apocryphal or canonical), born within the framework of more than ten centuries on Greek -and later Slavic -soil. All this provides grounds to assume that, from the point of view of its literary history, AI is one of the most important eschatological works of Byzantine and Slavonic medieval literary tradition.

## Abstract

At the crossroads of East and West, fifteenth-to seventeenth-century Crete became a remarkable laboratory of musical experimentation. records.description:
## Abstract

Greek colonisation in the Archaic period had as its goal the expansion and the exportation of a city state’s social and religious customs into different regions. Although the subject of Greek colonisation is often vague, and based on erroneous, and generous primary sources, which can confound links between the colonies and their apparent mother city, a connection can nevertheless be established between the colonies in the Black Sea and the mother city of Miletus through the religious institutions that were installed upon colonisation. The cult of the god Apollo was prevalent throughout the ancient Greek world during the Archaic, Classical and Hellenistic periods. For the Archaic period colonizing Greek city state of Miletus, Apollo was patron deity, the god of colonisation, as well as the god of seafaring.
